html:
"Western Masurian culture" is the map's label, from 500 BCE to 100 CE, for the Iron Age people of western Masuria, the lake district of what is now northeastern Poland, and nearby lands toward the Vistula.

Archaeologists usually place this area in the West Baltic Kurgans culture, which lasted from about 650 BCE into the first centuries CE across Masuria and the Sambian Peninsula. Its people buried the ashes of their dead under low round mounds ringed with stones. They lived in small farming villages and on hillforts, and some built houses on posts at the edges of lakes.

They spoke early Baltic languages. Their descendants were the Old Prussians and the Galindians; the geographer Ptolemy, in the 100s CE, names the Galindai in roughly this area. Amber gathered on the nearby Sambian coast made the region a source for the Amber Road to the Roman world.

Its neighbours on the map were the Pomeranian culture to the west and the Eastern Masurian culture to the east. In the 1200s this land was conquered by the Teutonic Knights, and over the following centuries the Prussians lost their language.
